Action Plan:
1. Start anti-inflammatory therapy for left elbow swelling: ibuprofen 400 mg, two times daily, take after food — route not documented; stop if heartburn develops.
2. Arrange blood tests (forms to be posted to patient) for inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatological antibodies, and gout screen. Results expected approximately 5–6 days after testing; patient to obtain bloods promptly when forms received.
3. Arrange follow-up to review clinical progress and blood results — follow-up may be face-to-face, telephone, or video per patient preference; patient to contact clinic after blood tests or sooner if symptoms change.
4. Safety-netting: urgent review (video/phone or in-person) if elbow becomes very red, very painful, or if redness spreads — this would require immediate assessment.
5. Send blood-test forms and schedule follow-up as above.
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: New swelling of the left elbow noticed ~1 week ago.
- Onset/duration/progression: Noted about one week ago; no preceding injury; not previously occurred.
- Symptoms/characteristics: Visible swelling at tip/underside of left elbow; slightly warm compared with adjacent skin; patient reports a sensation of fluid and a “weird” feeling adjacent to swelling; not painful at rest; can move elbow normally.
- Red flag symptoms denied at time of consult: no severe pain, no spreading redness, no systemic symptoms reported.
- Past medical history: Osteoarthritis diagnosed by GP a few years ago.
- Medications: None regular.
- Allergies: Peanuts (food allergy). No known medication allergies.
- Social history: Office-based job (desk work). Regular runner, exercises 2–3 times per week.

Objective:
- General: Patient alert and conversational (no systemic signs documented).
- Left elbow examination:
  - Visible swelling over tip/underside of left elbow.
  - Area slightly warm compared with surrounding skin.
  - Tip of elbow skin described as dry.
  - Tip of elbow not notably tender to direct pressure; adjacent area over swelling causes an abnormal sensation but not severe pain.
  - Full range of motion preserved; no limitation reported.
- Clinician impression on exam: findings do not appear consistent with septic arthritis at this time.
- Investigations: None performed during consultation. Blood tests planned (see Action Plan).

Assessment & Plan:

1. Left elbow swelling:
   - Assessment: Olecranon bursitis.
   - Differential diagnosis: Septic bursitis / septic arthritis; gout; cellulitis (considered).
   - Investigations planned: Blood tests — inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatological antibodies, and gout screen (forms to be sent to patient).
   - Treatment planned: Ibuprofen 400 mg, two times daily, after food — route not documented; stop if heartburn occurs.
   - Relevant referrals/arrangements: Follow-up appointment to review clinical status and blood results (phone/video or face-to-face per patient preference). Urgent review arranged if signs of worsening infection.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs not documented; exact route of ibuprofen not explicitly documented; no documentation of temperature, heart rate, or other systemic observations; no baseline blood test values (tests not yet performed); no imaging or aspiration performed.
- Internal conflicts from transcript: none identified.
- Transcript quality: Good — clear audio and complete history; minimal background noise; examination findings described adequately.
